proposals.explanation: Daimo (Daimo Pay) explicitly hides swap costs for a clean checkout and publishes no consumer-facing swap-fee disclosure; Walletbeat rates its fee transparency as unrated/unknown.
Daimo states swaps, bridges, and gas are hidden from users for a clean checkout and discloses no explicit bridging fee to the user.
No spread/markup disclosure is provided; the docs and site describe fees as hidden rather than showing any quote markup, and Walletbeat lists fee transparency as unrated.
No paid subscription or premium tier is offered on Daimo's site or docs; it is a per-transaction ramp/payment product with no subscription features.
Elytro supports in-app swaps but discloses no wallet swap fee on its site, FAQ, or GitHub, and Walletbeat rates its fee transparency as unassessable (https://beta.walletbeat.eth.limo/elytro/).
Elytro advertises in-app bridging ("Send, swap & bridge") but discloses no bridge fee anywhere on elytro.com, its FAQ, or GitHub (https://elytro.com/faq).
No spread or quote markup disclosure appears on Elytro's site, FAQ, or docs, and Walletbeat notes it lacks fee-transparency information for Elytro (https://beta.walletbeat.eth.limo/elytro/).
Elytro's FAQ states "The app and CLI are free," with only sponsored/network gas fees and no optional paid subscription or premium tier offered (https://elytro.com/faq).

Family's FAQ states it "does not charge any additional fees for using the wallet" and the swap-tokens support page only says users see "fees" without disclosing any specific swap-fee amount or percentage.
Family discloses no bridge/refuel fee; its FAQ states only network fees apply and no in-app bridge fee is published on its support pages.
Family publicly states it charges no additional wallet fees and sources best prices from various exchanges, with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral markup on swaps or ramps.
Family is offered as a free non-custodial wallet with no paid subscription or premium tier disclosed on its site, FAQ, or App Store listing.
Firefly is itself a hardware signing device (Firefly Pixie), and its minimal browser-based companion has no evidence of signing with other third-party hardware wallets.
Firefly is an air-gapped Ethereum signing device with no documented passkey/WebAuthn/FIDO verification factor.
Firefly is an offline air-gapped signer that relies on the paired browser/phone for network data and has no trust-minimized L1 light client.
Frame is a desktop dApp wallet with no built-in in-app swap feature; swaps are done via connected dApps/DEXs, so there is no Frame swap fee to disclose (https://frame.sh/).
Frame has no native in-app bridging feature; cross-chain transfers must be done through external services/dApps, so there is no Frame bridge fee to disclose (https://blog.frame.sh/frame-canary/).
Frame does not provide in-app swap/bridge quotes, so there is no price spread or markup applied by Frame to disclose (https://frame.sh/).

Frame is a free, open-source wallet that connects users directly to dApps/DEXs without an in-app swap/ramp order flow, so there is no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral revenue (https://frame.sh/).
Frame is offered as a free wallet with no subscription or premium paid tier mentioned on its site or docs (https://frame.sh/).

Safe{Wallet} help center discloses tiered native-swap widget fees (0.70% down to 0.1% for general pairs, 0.15%-0.05% for stablecoins) and states the fee percentage is always visible in the interface with a breakdown before approval.
Safe's native-bridge widget fee article discloses that the exact fee percentage is always known and displayed before confirming (e.g. a 0.1% widget fee = 1 USDT on a 1,000 USDT bridge).

The swap fee article discloses the pricing mechanics including price improvement/surplus (extra found by CoW Protocol is split between trader and protocol) and that network/liquidity-pool costs apply, rather than applying an undisclosed markup.

Fee revenue is transparently documented: the widget fee is paid to CoW Swap/LiFi with a portion going to the Safe Foundation as a license fee, and percentages are shown to the user, so there is no undisclosed partner/referral revenue.
Ambire's fee model is transparent, disclosing a flat swap/bridge fee with 100% of revenue used for $WALLET buybacks, with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral markup.
Ambire has no optional paid subscription or premium tier; fee reductions are tied to holding/staking $WALLET tokens rather than a paid subscription product.

Argent's support pages ('How does Argent make money' and 'All fees') disclose that it takes a share of the exchange fee on in-app crypto-to-crypto swaps via Paraswap/AVNU, with secondary sources citing ~0.5%.
Argent bridging relies on third-party bridges (Layerswap, Rhino.fi, StarkGate) and its docs state only network gas fees apply, with no disclosed Argent-charged bridge fee.
Argent transparently discloses its revenue as a share of the DEX-aggregator exchange fee, so partner/swap revenue is not undisclosed.
Argent/Ready offers an optional paid premium tier, Ready Metal, at 120 USDC/year with higher cashback and 0% FX vs the free Lite tier.
Coinbase's bridging help page discloses a 'Coinbase Fee' charged for bridging to networks other than Base, plus network transaction fees.
Reviews note the swap fee is embedded in the quoted rate rather than shown as a separate line item, and no official page discloses a specific spread/markup on quotes.
The 1% Coinbase swap fee and DEX-aggregator fees are documented on Coinbase's official pages, with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral revenue.
Base App is free with no subscription/premium tier within the wallet; Coinbase One is a separate Coinbase product not offered inside the app.
BitBox02 is itself a hardware signer; the BitBoxApp companion only pairs with BitBox devices and does not support signing with third-party hardware wallets.
BitBoxApp provides no known-malicious/phishing URL warning feature; its security model relies on manual on-device verification and its security-features page lists no such detection.
BitBoxApp does not warn on risky sends such as address poisoning or unknown recipients, instead instructing users to manually verify all transaction details on the device screen.
No evidence BitBoxApp flags interactions with known-malicious contracts; its security-features and send docs describe only on-device detail verification, not contract reputation checks.
BitBoxApp shows raw transaction details for on-device confirmation but does not simulate/preview net balance changes (no Blockaid/Blowfish-style simulation).
BitBox02's optional passphrase creates hidden wallets and can be used to set up a duress/decoy wallet with a small balance to reveal under coercion.
The BitBox02 Multi edition functions as a FIDO U2F authenticator for two-factor authentication on websites like Google and GitHub.
BitBoxApp connects to backend/RPC nodes (or a user's own full node for Bitcoin) and provides no trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client verification.

Bitget Wallet discloses a swap service fee (~0.3% via its Super DEX aggregator) with transparent quotes shown before transactions, per the Coin Bureau review and Bitget's own swap materials stating the fee is shown before completing any transaction.
Bridge/provider fees for cross-chain transactions are displayed transparently in the quote before execution in Bitget Wallet's Super DEX interface, per the Coin Bureau review.
Sources indicate Bitget Wallet uses transparent upfront quotes for swap/bridge fees with no evidence of undisclosed partner markups or rate mark-ups, so no hidden partner revenue is indicated.
Reviews of Bitget Wallet describe no optional paid subscription or premium membership tier for the wallet itself (only a tiered card cashback program), indicating no subscription features.

Brave discloses its swap fee policy, stating in its help center and blog that Brave does not add its own fees to in-wallet swaps (its former swap fee was removed in v1.67.x, tracked in brave-browser issue #38566).
Brave's cross-chain swaps blog and help center clearly state 'Brave does not add fees to swaps or bridges performed within Brave Wallet,' disclosing its bridge fee policy.
Brave publicly states it does not add fees to swaps or bridges and removed its former swap fee, indicating a transparent fee model with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral revenue.
Brave Wallet is entirely free with no paid subscription or premium tier for the wallet itself (Brave's premium products like VPN/Leo are separate non-wallet services).
Coinbase Wallet clearly discloses and charges a 1% fee on in-app token swaps, shown before confirming and documented across Coinbase Wallet fee references.
The swap fee model is transparent (flat 1% disclosed at transaction time), with no evidence of undisclosed partner markup or referral kickbacks.
The self-custody Coinbase Wallet does not offer its own paid premium tier; Coinbase One is a subscription for the separate Coinbase exchange app rather than the wallet's features.
Cypherock X1 is itself a hardware signer and its cySync companion app only signs with the X1 device, not third-party hardware wallets.
cySync provides on-device address verification but no automated risky-send warnings such as address poisoning or new-recipient alerts are documented.
cySync relies on manual review of permissions on the Vault screen and offers no automated malicious-contract flagging.
cySync shows transaction details for on-device verification but does not simulate/preview net balance changes before signing.
No evidence Cypherock X1 or cySync uses passkeys/WebAuthn/FIDO; it uses card-tap plus PIN for verification.
cySync relies on standard RPC/backend for account and history data with no trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client.

Exodus's official 'How does Exodus make money' support page and swap UI disclose that it earns via the spread and shows the exact amount you pay/receive (fixed rate from ~0.5%) before confirming a swap.

Exodus openly discloses on its official support page that it earns from the swap spread and receives a small share of third-party fiat providers' processing fees, and it shows the full quote (spread) before confirmation, so the revenue is not undisclosed.
Gem Wallet's swap-fees FAQ explicitly discloses it takes no service/handling fees or commissions and that swap provider/protocol fees are factored into the quoted rate visible before confirming.
Gem Wallet integrates cross-chain bridges (Across, THORChain) but its docs do not itemize or disclose any specific bridge fee it charges, only a general 'save on fees' claim.
The swap page states 'There are no hidden charges or inflated spreads - you can see all costs before confirming the transaction,' explicitly addressing spread/markup.
Gem Wallet's docs state it takes no commissions/markup and no affiliate program, and quotes disclose all costs before confirmation, indicating no undisclosed partner revenue.
Gem Wallet is a free open-source self-custody wallet with no premium/paid subscription tier documented across its site and knowledge base.
The Lattice1 is itself a hardware signer used with software wallets like MetaMask/Frame; its companion tooling does not sign with other third-party hardware wallets.
The Lattice1 uses ABI decoding to make calldata human-readable but does not flag/blocklist known-malicious contracts; it relies on the user reading the decoded data.
The Lattice1 provides ABI-decoded clear signing of raw transaction data but does not simulate/predict net balance changes before signing.
The Lattice1 supports an optional BIP39 passphrase (a 25th word) that generates a separate hidden wallet, functioning as a decoy/hidden-wallet mechanism.
The Lattice1 uses a device PIN and SafeCard PIN for authentication with no mention of passkeys/WebAuthn/FIDO in its security documentation.
The Lattice1 relies on connected software wallets/RPCs for chain state and provides no trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client.
imKey Pro is itself a hardware signer whose companion app (imToken) is used to activate/pair the imKey device, not to sign with third-party hardware wallets.
imToken automatically hides high-risk address-poisoning transactions and shows a security reminder when a user copies an address from transaction history.
imToken tags risky tokens/contracts as 'Warning' (pops a security alert on transfer) and hides 'Risk/High Risk' tokens to protect users from malicious contracts.
imKey runs a public 'Vulnerability and Threat Intelligence Bounty Program' and imToken runs a bounty program with SlowMist.
imKey Pro documentation describes only a standard 6-8 digit PIN (auto-reset after 5 failed attempts) with no passphrase-based hidden wallet or decoy/duress mode.
imToken/imKey rely on RPC nodes for chain state with no indication of a trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client.
imToken's in-app swaps run through Tokenlon, whose published fees page discloses a 0.3% trade fee (0.04% for stablecoins, tiered down to 0.10%).
imToken's help center documents cross-chain bridging via Celer cBridge (0%–0.04%) and other bridges with their fee structures explained per protocol.
imToken's swap fee model is transparently published via Tokenlon's public fees page and its help center, with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral markups.
imToken is a free wallet with no paid subscription or premium tier; reviews and its site indicate no subscription requirement or premium features.

Keycard Shell is itself an air-gapped hardware signer with no mandatory companion app (it pairs with third-party software wallets), so signing with a different third-party hardware wallet is not applicable.
Keycard Shell has no companion app and its docs/security pages describe only air-gapped signing and blind-signing minimization, with no known-malicious/phishing URL warning feature.
The device offers on-screen transaction verification but no documented risky-send/address-poisoning warnings, and it has no companion app to provide them.
No malicious/flagged-contract warning feature is documented for Keycard Shell, which relies on third-party wallets for such checks and only aims to 'minimize blind signing'.
Keycard Shell shows transaction details for verification on-device but does not simulate net balance changes, and it has no companion app providing simulation.
Keycard's About page links a 'Security & vulnerability disclosure (IFT)' program run under the Institute of Free Technology, which operates a HackenProof bug bounty covering its projects.
Neither Keycard's security/about pages nor its GitHub repo mention passkey/WebAuthn/FIDO verification; the device uses PIN plus secure-element key storage.
As an offline air-gapped signer with no companion app, Keycard Shell provides no Ethereum L1 light-client verification and relies on the connected software wallet's RPC.
Keystone 3 Pro is itself a hardware signer that works via QR/third-party wallets and has no companion app that signs with other third-party hardware wallets, so this is not applicable.
Keystone decodes and displays full transaction/contract details on-device (anti-blind-signing) but there is no evidence of net-balance-change simulation like Blockaid/Blowfish.
Keystone supports an optional passphrase 'hidden vault' for plausible deniability, with a default sentinel wallet shown under duress while assets stay in passphrase-protected wallets.
Keystone 3 Pro uses PIN/fingerprint and QR-based device verification; no source indicates passkey/WebAuthn/FIDO2 as a verification factor.
Keystone is an air-gapped cold signer relying on connected third-party wallets/RPCs and provides no trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client.
Ledger is itself a hardware signing device; Ledger Live is its companion app and does not sign with third-party hardware wallets.
Ledger Live's Transaction Check (powered by Blockaid) flags interactions with questionable dApps/scam sites as potential risks or critical threats before signing.
Transaction Check flags sending assets to an unknown address as a potential risk before the transaction is signed.
Transaction Check via Blockaid identifies transactions involving malicious contracts or stolen funds and flags them as critical threats.
Ledger's Transaction Check simulates the transaction and validates its outcomes (via Blockaid/Tenderly/Cyvers) before signing.
Ledger's passphrase feature creates hidden wallets for plausible deniability, letting a user reveal only a decoy standard account under coercion.
Ledger devices run a Security Key application implementing FIDO U2F/FIDO2/WebAuthn for use as a 2FA/MFA authentication factor.
Ledger Live relies on standard/third-party RPC providers and Ledger's own backend rather than a trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client; no such feature is documented.
MetaMask's support user-guide page explicitly discloses a 0.875% MetaMask swap service fee in its fee breakdown.
MetaMask's support page 'How are bridge fees calculated?' discloses a 0.875% MetaMask fee applied on each bridge transaction.
MetaMask openly publishes its 0.875% swap and bridge fees in support docs, indicating a transparent fee model rather than undisclosed partner markup.
MetaMask offers paid subscription tiers including Transaction Shield ($9.99/month security subscription) and the Metal Card annual membership ($199/yr).
Mt Pelerin's pricing page discloses swap fees: first CHF 500/year free, then 0.5% commission (0.1% for USDC-to-USDC swaps).
Bridging is disclosed as using the same swap fee model (free up to CHF 500/year, or CHF 1,000 if referred, then standard exchange fees) on the bridge/USDT pages.
The swap page explicitly discloses its spread policy, stating swaps occur 'with no spread, no slippage, and no price impact' at the real market price minus a transparent service fee.

Mt Pelerin discloses its fee model transparently ('zero hidden costs minus a small, transparent service fee') with published commission percentages, and no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral markup was found.
Mt Pelerin offers an MPS shareholder token tier that raises the free-volume allowance up to CHF 50,000/year and grants discounted fees, functioning as an optional premium tier.

NGRAVE ZERO is itself a hardware signer and its LIQUID companion app does not sign with third-party hardware wallets (it interoperates with software wallets MetaMask/Rabby), so this is categorically not applicable.
NGRAVE documents that a passphrase creates a hidden wallet and a small-balance passphrase wallet can act as a duress/decoy wallet surrendered under coercion.
LIQUID is a portfolio/broadcast app relying on standard RPC/QR flow with no documented trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client.

NuFi's Cardano exchange support article states users need ADA to pay a transaction fee 'plus a service fee for using the swap functionality,' but no fee amount or percentage is disclosed, and the Jupiter DEX swap article discloses no NuFi fee at all.
Multiple reviews indicate NuFi is free with no premium tiers or subscription features, and no official NuFi page advertises a paid tier.
OKX publishes a DEX fees page disclosing the interface fee on in-app swaps (0% to 0.5% depending on token group).
OKX transparently publishes its DEX/interface fee schedule and shows all costs before confirmation, indicating no undisclosed partner/referral markup.
No evidence of an optional paid subscription or premium tier for OKX Wallet was found across official pages and reviews; it is a free self-custody wallet monetized via swap fees.
OneKey Pro is itself a hardware signer and its companion app manages OneKey devices rather than third-party hardware wallets, so this metric is not applicable.
SignGuard integrates GoPlus, Blockaid and ScamSniffer to warn on interaction with malicious/flagged contracts before signing.
The OneKey app simulates transactions and displays key details (methods, approval amounts, target addresses) with Blockaid-powered clear signing before signing.
OneKey supports passphrase-based hidden wallets attachable to a secondary PIN, providing plausible deniability under coercion.
OneKey hardware wallets support FIDO and FIDO2 (WebAuthn/passkey) authentication as a security key.
No evidence found that OneKey verifies Ethereum L1 state with a trust-minimized light client; it relies on RPC providers.
Phantom's official help documentation discloses a 0.85% swap fee (shown in the fee disclosure before confirmation) on in-app swaps.
Phantom's cross-chain swap/bridge quote screen discloses Phantom's fee plus the bridge provider fee and network fees before the user confirms.
Phantom transparently discloses its 0.85% platform fee and bridge/aggregator fees in-app and in help docs, so there is no evidence of undisclosed partner revenue.
Neither PillarX's site, developer docs (docs.pillarx.app), nor its App Store listing disclose any fee charged on in-app swaps/Offers Engine, so the swap fee is not clearly disclosed.
PillarX offers cross-chain swaps but no official page discloses any bridging fee it charges; the docs cover only dapp development, not fees.
No PillarX page discloses any price spread or markup applied on swap quotes from its aggregator/Offers Engine.
The App Store listing shows PillarX as free with no in-app purchases, and no site/docs material mentions any paid subscription or premium tier.
Rabby officially announced and displays a 0.25% fee on its built-in swap, shown in the quote before execution.
Rabby's fee model is transparent (explicit 0.25% swap fee disclosed publicly and in-app), with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral markups.
Rabby is a free wallet monetized via the 0.25% swap fee and gas top-up service fee, with no optional paid subscription or premium tier found.
Rainbow's support page states the "Rainbow Fee" (the percentage/amount Rainbow applies) is always visible on the review screen before swapping.
The same Bridge and Swap support page discloses that the Rainbow Fee is shown on the review screen for both bridging and swapping transactions.
Rainbow presents its fee transparently as a visible "Rainbow Fee" line item on the review screen, with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral markup.
Rainbow is a free wallet with no paid subscription or premium tier; only network gas and disclosed swap fees apply.
Trezor is itself a hardware signer and Trezor Suite does not support signing with third-party hardware wallets like Ledger.
Trezor Suite detects address-poisoning and airdrop scam tokens, blurring them and labeling transactions as unverified/phishing.
Trezor's guidance directs users to external tools like Etherscan's token approval checker and offers no built-in flagged/malicious-contract warning before signing.
Trezor Suite has users review raw transaction/EIP-712 data on the device but does not simulate net balance changes before signing.
Trezor Model T and Safe family devices work as FIDO2/passkey security keys for phishing-resistant 2FA and passwordless login.
Trezor Suite relies on backend/RPC data rather than an embedded trust-minimized Ethereum L1 light client to verify state.

Trust Wallet publicly markets swaps as having no wallet fee (only DEX spread ~0.5-1% baked into the rate), yet its Premium program offers 'swap fee discounts,' so the actual wallet swap fee is not clearly disclosed as a stated percentage.
Trust Premium is a free loyalty/rewards program that explicitly states 'There are no subscriptions or hidden fees,' so there is no optional paid subscription or premium paid tier.

Uniswap Labs publishes a dedicated support page disclosing its swap/interface fee and shows any applicable fee in the in-app swap detail section (paid in the output token), so the fee/markup is clearly disclosed.
Uniswap's fee model is transparent (Labs fee documented and shown in the swap detail section, plus disclosed protocol/LP fee tiers), with no evidence of undisclosed partner/referral markup.
Uniswap Wallet is a free non-custodial app (iOS, Android, browser extension) with no advertised optional paid subscription or premium tier.
Zerion's official help center 'Understanding Fees on Zerion' page discloses a 0.67% service fee applied to in-app swaps.
Zerion discloses its bridge fee in the help center and blog (e.g., 0.8% bridge fee announced in the Zerion Fee Update for Bridge).
Zerion transparently publishes its swap (0.67%) and bridge (0.8%) service fees on its official help center, indicating a disclosed rather than hidden revenue model.
Zerion offers a paid Premium subscription (~$99/year) providing advanced analytics and reduced trading/bridging fees.
Zeus is an open-source self-custodial wallet that routes swaps directly through Uniswap's Universal Router with no wallet-level swap fee documented and no fees page disclosing one.
Bridging is done directly via the Across protocol with no wallet-level bridge fee documented or disclosed in the repository.
The wallet uses on-chain Uniswap quotes directly and there is no disclosed price spread or markup applied to quotes.
The open-source code routes swaps/bridges directly to Uniswap and Across with no referral/partner code documented, showing no evidence of undisclosed partner revenue.
Zeus is a free MIT-licensed open-source wallet with no optional paid subscription or premium tier offered.
Coinbase Wallet shows a Bridge Fee and Coinbase Fee in the transaction summary before the user confirms a cross-chain bridge, per the official Coinbase Help bridging page.
Exodus XO Swap displays the full quote and fixed rate before the user confirms a cross-chain swap/bridge, so users see the amount received beforehand.
NuFi supports cross-chain bridging via SwapKit/THORChain but no official source confirms bridge fees are explicitly disclosed before confirmation.
OKX's official OKX Bridge guide states all costs — bridge fee (0.08–0.2%) and network gas — are displayed before confirming the transaction.
Rabby uses LI.FI bridge aggregation with a 0.25% fee, and its pre-confirmation simulation surfaces the expected fee cost before the user bridges.
Trust Wallet's official bridging guide instructs users to review the fees associated with the transaction before confirming.

Insufficient public information to determine whether Daimo takes undisclosed partner revenue; swap/bridge fees are described as bundled for a clean checkout but no specific kickback arrangement was confirmed.
No official documentation found addressing Elytro partner revenue or affiliate arrangements; unrated for fee transparency on Walletbeat.
NuFi discloses that it earns referral fees from integrated on-ramps and swap aggregators; no evidence of undisclosed/hidden partner revenue was found.

PillarX integrates StealthEX (which runs an affiliate program) but no documented evidence confirms whether PillarX takes affiliate revenue or discloses it; treated as unknown rather than asserting an undocumented negative claim.

Trust Wallet discloses at a high level that it earns affiliate commissions on swaps/staking, but specific partner arrangements are not detailed and no clear evidence of undisclosed kickbacks was found.
Ambire publicly discloses a 0.5% swap and bridge fee and states wallet fees are made transparent to the user before confirmation.
Argent's official support page discloses a 0.5% exchange fee on swaps, shown in-app before confirming.
Brave's official support docs state swap fees are displayed transparently, with only network gas and the disclosed swap fee applied.
Family's FAQ states it charges no additional wallet fees and shows estimated fees before confirmation, but does not disclose any platform spread or markup percentage.
imToken integrates Tokenlon (0.1–0.15% fees) and shows a swap cost warning, but explicit spread/markup disclosure before confirmation could not be confirmed from official sources.
NuFi states it charges no swap fees (only network fees), routing through aggregators; the underlying aggregator spread is not separately surfaced to the user.
Rabby's official account announced a 0.25% built-in swap fee, and the swap flow previews the expected received amount including fee before confirmation.
Rainbow's official support page states the Rainbow Fee is always visible on the review page before confirming a swap.
Zerion's official help center discloses a 0.67% service fee on swaps and states there are no hidden fees, with network and exchange fees also disclosed.
Safe Wallet is free for core functionality (signer management, transaction proposal/execution) and does not charge for wallet use per the reviewed pricing.
Base App (formerly Coinbase Wallet) shows swap fees (up to ~1% Coinbase fee) on the confirmation screen before the user confirms the swap.
Firefly is a minimal DIY air-gapped Ethereum signer; its documented feature set (multi-sig, offline signing, recovery) includes no malicious-contract registry or blocklist.
Keystone's documentation focuses on air-gapped clear-signing and secure elements; no blocklist-based malicious-contract warning is described for the device or companion apps.
NGRAVE ZERO is fully air-gapped and relies on manual QR-based verification; no malicious-contract registry/blocklist warning is documented.
Firefly's documented features cover multi-sig, offline signing and recovery only; no flagged-address blacklist or address-poisoning detection is described.
GridPlus Lattice1 security docs describe clear signing and tamper protection but no blacklisted-address or address-poisoning send warning.
Keystone firmware includes address-poisoning detection that flags transactions to addresses resembling previous destinations before signing.
NGRAVE ZERO documentation describes no blacklisted-address or address-poisoning warning; it relies on manual verification on the secure display before QR signing.
OneKey's SignGuard (GoPlus/Blockaid/ScamSniffer) detects hidden malicious addresses and flags suspicious approvals with risk alerts before signing.
Cypherock's security docs focus on seedless design and secure elements; no blocklist-based phishing/dApp URL warning is documented for the X1 or cySync app.
Firefly is a bare DIY signer with no network connectivity or companion app implementing URL scanning.
GridPlus Lattice1 security docs cover hardware protection and clear signing only; no phishing-URL blocklist or dApp scam warning is described.
imKey's companion app imToken bans risky dApp URLs and shows DApp access risk reminders for high-risk sites, providing blocklist-based scam URL warnings.
Keystone's own blog recommends third-party tools like ScamSniffer for phishing protection rather than a built-in URL blocklist in the device or companion apps.
NGRAVE ZERO is fully air-gapped; neither the device nor the LIQUID companion app documents a blocklist-based phishing/scam URL warning.
OneKey's SignGuard integrates GoPlus/Blockaid/ScamSniffer to detect phishing sites and malicious dApps in real time with alerts before signing.
Trezor Suite's WalletConnect integration warns when a dApp is unverified or flagged as dangerous before the user connects/signs.
The Firefly DIY wallet displays only raw transaction parameters on its OLED screen; no transaction simulation or balance-change preview is documented.
imKey Pro shows amount, recipient and fee for manual verification before signing, but no transaction simulation of net effects is documented.
NGRAVE's own blind-signing article notes smart-contract details cannot always be decoded on ZERO; simulation is not a feature of the device itself.
Cypherock X1's feature spec lists a Dummy/Decoy/Duress wallet enabled via multiple BIP-39 passphrase-derived wallets with separate PINs, for coercion protection.
Firefly's repository and documentation contain no mention of a duress mode, decoy PIN, or passphrase-derived hidden wallet.
SatoshiLabs' official Trezor blog names plausible deniability as a benefit of the passphrase/hidden-wallet feature, describing revealing a decoy wallet under coercion.
imKey Pro authenticates via PIN and Bluetooth/USB; no WebAuthn/FIDO2 passkey support is documented for the crypto wallet (the imKey Pass S6 is a separate FIDO2 product).
NGRAVE ZERO authenticates via an 8-digit PIN and fingerprint; no passkey/WebAuthn/FIDO2 authentication is documented.
